newsitem.title: GERMANY: German reform focus shifts from taxes to pensions.
newsitem.headline: German reform focus shifts from taxes to pensions.

text.p: The spotlight in Germany's reform debate shifted on Monday to how to finance the country's old-age pensions scheme into the next century without upsetting plans by Chancellor Helmut Kohl's coalition to slash taxes.
Labour Minister Norbert Bluem chaired a final meeting of a policy group expected to propose a cut in state pensions to 63 percent of average net pay from 70 percent to contain costs.

But Bluem's bid to remodel the compulsory pensions scheme to cope with the "greying" of Germany's 80 million population has run headlong into Finance Minister Theo Waigel's bid to slash 30 billion marks ($18 billion) in taxes to boost investment and jobs.
Waigel last week unveiled plans to cut income and corporate taxes, mainly in 1999, while scrapping tax breaks which hit revenue collection and hamper investment and job creation.

But Bluem objected to Waigel's plan to tax pensions, and has threatened to hold up his pensions reform if he doesn't get a two-point hike in the 15 percent rate of value-added tax to help bail out the strained pay-as-you-go pension scheme.
Kohl's government this year put up pension contributions -- paid half by employers and half by workers -- to a record 20.3 percent of wages after cash reserves ran dangerously low.

To prevent a cost explosion, Bluem wants extra VAT revenues to cover unrelated costs -- like jobs training, maternity benefits and compensation for war victims -- now carried by people paying monthly pensions contributions.

Although Bluem, Kohl's longest serving minister, was among a minority of the Christian Democrat (CDU) party leadership who voted against Waigel's tax proposal, government leaders and pensions experts on Monday rallied to support him.

"Norbert Bluem has a very tough task to master with the reform of the social security and in particularly the pensions system. But he has our full support," CDU parliamentary leader Wolfgang Schaeuble told Monday's Bild newspaper.
Schaeuble did, however, call Bluem's linking of the tax and pensions issues "unfortunate".

He also told Bild he would not be drawn into a game of "Russian roulette" over how much to raise VAT, but did not rule out increasing other indirect levies -- like petrol tax -- to help finance social security reforms.
